title: Entropy
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 7
summary:
Entropy turns the second law from a set of statements into a **property you can compute**. It starts from the **Clausius inequality**, $\oint \delta Q/T \le 0$: integrated around any cycle, the heat-over-temperature is zero for a reversible cycle and negative otherwise. The reversible case lets us define entropy by $dS = (\delta Q/T)_{int,rev}$. Because $S$ is a property, $\Delta S$ between two states is fixed by the endpoints alone — you may compute it along any convenient reversible path, even if the real process was messy.

The headline result is the **increase-of-entropy principle**: the entropy of an *isolated* system can only increase or, at best (reversible), stay the same. For any system plus its surroundings, $S_{gen} = \Delta S_{total} \ge 0$. Entropy generation $S_{gen}$ measures irreversibility: zero for a reversible process, positive for a real one, never negative. A process with $S_{gen} < 0$ is impossible.

To actually evaluate $\Delta s$ we use the **$T\,ds$ (Gibbs) relations**, $T\,ds = du + P\,dv$ and $T\,ds = dh - v\,dP$. Integrating them for an **ideal gas** with constant specific heats gives two interchangeable forms: $\Delta s = c_v\ln(T_2/T_1) + R\ln(v_2/v_1)$ and $\Delta s = c_p\ln(T_2/T_1) - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$ — pick whichever matches the variables you're given. For an **incompressible** solid or liquid it simplifies to $\Delta s = c\ln(T_2/T_1)$.

A process that is both adiabatic and reversible has $\Delta s = 0$ — it is **isentropic**, the ideal model for turbines, compressors, pumps and nozzles. For an ideal gas with constant specific heats, isentropic states are linked by $T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)^{(k-1)/k} = (v_1/v_2)^{k-1}$ and $Pv^k = \text{const}$. Real devices fall short, and the gap is quantified by **isentropic efficiency**: for a turbine $\eta_T = (h_1 - h_2)/(h_1 - h_{2s})$ (actual drop ÷ ideal drop); for a compressor the ratio inverts.

Finally, the **entropy balance**, $S_{in} - S_{out} + S_{gen} = \Delta S_{system}$, with entropy transported by heat as $\sum Q_k/T_k$, ties it all together — the second-law counterpart of the energy balance, and the tool for finding $S_{gen}$ in any device. The workflow: pick the right $\Delta s$ form for the substance and given data; for ideal devices set $\Delta s = 0$; for real ones, use isentropic efficiency or the entropy balance.

equations.name: Clausius inequality & entropy definition
equations.useWhen: Establishing entropy as a property and computing $\Delta S$ for heat exchange at a known temperature (e.g. a reservoir at constant $T$).
equations.note: Equality holds for reversible cycles; "<" for irreversible ones.

equations.name: Increase-of-entropy principle
equations.useWhen: Judging feasibility and measuring irreversibility. Compute the total entropy change of system + surroundings; it must be $\ge 0$.
equations.note: Entropy is NOT conserved — it is generated by irreversibility.

equations.name: T ds (Gibbs) relations
equations.latex: T\,ds = du + P\,dv, \qquad T\,ds = dh - v\,dP
equations.useWhen: The starting point for deriving every $\Delta s$ formula. Use the $du$ form with volume data, the $dh$ form with pressure data.
equations.note: These connect entropy to measurable properties; integrate them for each substance type.

equations.name: Entropy change of an ideal gas
equations.useWhen: Any ideal-gas process. Choose the $(T,v)$ form or the $(T,P)$ form to match the data you're given. Temperatures in K.
equations.note: Constant specific heats assumed. For high accuracy use the tabulated $s^\circ(T)$ function instead.

equations.name: Entropy change of an incompressible substance
equations.useWhen: Heating or cooling a solid or liquid. No pressure term — volume barely changes. Temperatures in K.
equations.note: Isentropic ($\Delta s = 0$) for an incompressible substance means $T_2 = T_1$.

equations.name: Isentropic ideal-gas relations
equations.useWhen: An ideal gas undergoes a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) process — the ideal model for turbines, compressors, nozzles. Find the ideal exit state.
equations.note: Constant specific heats, $k = c_p/c_v$. Temperatures and pressures absolute.

equations.name: Isentropic efficiency
equations.useWhen: Relating a real adiabatic device to its ideal isentropic counterpart. Turbine: actual ÷ ideal work. Compressor/pump: ideal ÷ actual work.
equations.note: $h_{2s}$ is the exit enthalpy of the *ideal* (isentropic, $s_2 = s_1$) process to the same exit pressure.

equations.name: Entropy balance
rearrangements: \dot S_{gen} = \sum \dot m_{out} s_{out} - \sum \dot m_{in} s_{in} - \sum \frac{\dot Q_k}{T_k}
equations.useWhen: Finding entropy generation in any closed or open system — the second-law analog of the energy balance.
equations.note: Entropy enters/leaves with heat ($Q/T$) and with mass ($\dot m s$), and is *generated* internally by irreversibility.

glossary.definition: A property defined by $dS = (\delta Q/T)_{int,rev}$, measuring disorder / the unavailability of energy for work. Units kJ/K (specific: kJ/(kg·K)).
$\oint \delta Q/T \le 0$ for any cycle; the basis for defining entropy as a property.
Entropy created by irreversibilities within a system; $\ge 0$ always, $= 0$ only for reversible processes.
The total entropy of an isolated system (or system + surroundings) can never decrease: $S_{gen} \ge 0$.
$T\,ds = du + P\,dv$ and $T\,ds = dh - v\,dP$; relate entropy to other properties and generate the working $\Delta s$ formulas.
A reversible + adiabatic process, for which $\Delta s = 0$ ($s_2 = s_1$). The ideal model for turbines, pumps, nozzles, compressors.
$k = c_p/c_v$; appears in the isentropic ideal-gas relations.
Ratio comparing a real adiabatic device to its isentropic ideal — actual/ideal work for a turbine, ideal/actual for a compressor.
$S_{in} - S_{out} + S_{gen} = \Delta S_{system}$; the second-law bookkeeping equation, used to find $S_{gen}$.
Heat carries entropy $Q/T$ across a boundary; work carries none. Mass flow carries $\dot m s$.
For an ideal gas with constant specific heats: $T_2/T_1 = (P_2/P_1)^{(k-1)/k} = (v_1/v_2)^{k-1}$ and $Pv^k = $ const.

tips: **Two ideal-gas $\Delta s$ forms — match them to your data.** Given $T$ and $v$? Use $c_v\ln(T_2/T_1) + R\ln(v_2/v_1)$. Given $T$ and $P$? Use $c_p\ln(T_2/T_1) - R\ln(P_2/P_1)$.
**Isentropic = reversible AND adiabatic → $s_2 = s_1$.** Set entropy equal at inlet and outlet to find the ideal exit state, *then* apply isentropic efficiency for the real device.

**$h_{2s}$ vs $h_2$.** $h_{2s}$ is the ideal (isentropic) exit enthalpy at the actual exit pressure; $h_2$ is the real one. Turbine efficiency = actual drop $(h_1-h_2)$ over ideal drop $(h_1-h_{2s})$.
**Entropy is generated, not conserved.** Unlike energy, $S_{gen} > 0$ for real processes. A computed $S_{gen} < 0$ means an error or an impossible process.
**All logs take absolute temperatures (K).** Every $\ln(T_2/T_1)$ uses kelvin; a ratio of °C values is wrong.
**Don't confuse adiabatic with isentropic.** Adiabatic ($Q=0$) is isentropic only if it is *also* reversible. A throttling valve is adiabatic but generates entropy.
